morphology.shape: Filamentous mold with radiating conidial heads
morphology.notes: Yellow-green, granular conidial heads; uniseriate or biseriate phialides bearing chains of conidia

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil, decaying vegetation, and stored grains/nuts worldwide
habitat.hostAssociation: Environmental saprophyte and important agricultural contaminant; opportunistic human pathogen
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Common contaminant of stored corn, peanuts, and other crops, particularly in warm, humid conditions

microscopy.appearance: Septate hyphae with rough-walled conidiophores and radiating chains of yellow-green conidia

culture.growthCharacteristics: Rapid growth at room temperature and 37°C

identificationClues: Yellow-green colony color on Sabouraud agar
Best known outside clinical microbiology as the major producer of aflatoxin, a potent carcinogenic mycotoxin, in contaminated crops
Second most common cause of invasive aspergillosis after A. fumigatus

diseases: Invasive aspergillosis (second most common causative species after A. fumigatus)
clinicalImportance.transmission: Inhalation of airborne conidia; direct inoculation (e.g. corneal trauma) for keratitis
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Agriculturally significant as the primary source of aflatoxin contamination in stored grains/nuts (a major food-safety and public-health concern in some regions); clinically an important though less common cause of invasive aspergillosis than A. fumigatus
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Species-level identification distinguishing it from A. fumigatus and A. niger matters because of differing antifungal susceptibility patterns

examFacts.importantTest: Lactophenol cotton blue mount; colony morphology
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Major natural producer of aflatoxin, a potent carcinogen found in contaminated crops
